title: Sweet potato scones
subtitle: Moist, lightly spiced scones made with mashed sweet potato
excerpt: Sweet potato adds moisture and colour to a standard scone dough, which means less butter is needed and the scones keep softer for longer than a plain version. The cinnamon is restrained; these are not overly sweet and work equally well with jam or with butter and cheese.
sourceNotes: Sweet potato scones draw on North American and Scottish baking traditions, where root vegetables have been used in bread and scone doughs since the eighteenth century to extend flour and add moisture. The combination of sweet potato and cinnamon in baked goods became widespread in twentieth century UK and American baking.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze baked and cooled scones. Reheat from frozen at 170 degrees Celsius for 12 minutes.
recipe.batchNotes: Double the recipe easily; the mashed sweet potato can be made a day ahead.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: These keep better than plain scones because the sweet potato retains moisture. Best within 2 days.

baking.bakeTemperatureNote: Conventional oven, 200 degrees Celsius. Fan oven: 185 degrees Celsius. Slightly lower than standard scones because the sweet potato in the dough has more moisture to drive off.

glossaryTerms.definition: Root vegetables like sweet potato or pumpkin add both water and starch to a scone dough. The extra moisture means less added liquid is needed, and the extra starch slows staling so the scones stay soft longer. The vegetable must be mashed very smoothly; any lumps will create weak points where the scone tears as it rises.

content.text: The sweet potato must be baked or steamed, not boiled, before mashing; boiling adds too much extra water and makes the dough unworkably sticky. Understanding
helps you judge how much milk to add; the dough should be soft but not wet.

items.prepNote: baked or steamed until tender, mashed smooth and cooled

content.text: Preheat the oven to 200 degrees Celsius. Line a baking tray with baking paper.

Whisk together the flour, baking powder, cinnamon, salt, and sugar. Add the cold butter and rub in very briefly; leave the butter in rough pea-sized pieces. Stir in the mashed sweet potato, then add the milk a little at a time, mixing with a fork until the dough just comes together. It should be soft and slightly sticky but not wet. Add an extra splash of milk if the dough feels dry.
Tip gently onto a floured surface and press to 3 cm thickness. Cut out rounds using a 6 cm cutter, pressing straight down. Re-press once only.

Place on the tray with the sides touching (this helps them rise straight). Brush the tops with milk. Bake for 13 to 15 minutes until risen and deep golden on top. Cool briefly before serving with butter.
